'''''Caryota mitis''''', known as the '''clustering fishtail palm''' or '''fishtail palm''', is a species of palm native to [[Tropical Asia]] from [[India]] to [[Java]] to southern [[China]], now sparingly naturalized in southern [[Florida]] and in parts of Africa and Latin America.<ref>Berendsohn, W.G., A. K. Gruber & J. A. Monterrosa Salomón. 2012. Nova Silva Cuscatlanica. Árboles nativos e introducidos de El Salvador. Parte 2: Angiospermae – Familias M a P y Pteridophyta. Englera 29(2): 1–300.</ref><ref>Idárraga-Piedrahita, A., R. D. C. Ortiz, R. Callejas Posada & M. Merello. (eds.) 2011. Flora de Antioquia: Catálogo de las Plantas Vasculares 2: 9–939. Universidad de Antioquia, Medellín.</ref><ref>Linares, J. L. 2003 [2005]. Listado comentado de los árboles nativos y cultivados en la república de El Salvador. Ceiba 44(2): 105–268.</ref><ref>Molina Rosito, A. 1975. Enumeración de las plantas de Honduras. Ceiba 19(1): 1–118.</ref><ref>ORSTOM. 1988. List of Vascular Plants of Gabon with Synonymy, Herbier National du Gabon, Yaounde.</ref> The species was originally described from [[Vietnam]] in 1790.<ref name="asdfkljasdfh8owe"/> In Florida, it grows in [[hummocks]] and in disturbed wooded areas.<ref>Wunderlin, R. P. 1998. Guide to the Vascular Plants of Florida i–x, 1–806. University Press of Florida, Gainesville.</ref>

== Botany ==
[[File:叢立孔雀椰子 20190606204454 02.jpg |thumb|Leaf of a fishtail palm.]]

''Caryota mitis'' has clustered stems up to 10 m (33 feet) tall and 15 cm (6 inches) in diameter.<ref name="FoNA">{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200027070 |title=Caryota mitis  |date=n.d. |website= Flora of North America |publisher=eFloras |access-date=8 February 2014<!-- fr pg hstry -->}}</ref> Leaves can be up to 3 m (10 feet) long. Each leaf is made of many pairs of leaflets shaped like [[caudal fin|tail fin]]s that give this palm its name.<ref name="WS">{{cite web |last1=Tan |first1=Ria |date=October 2016 |title= Fishtail palm  |url=http://www.wildsingapore.com/wildfacts/plants/coastal/caryota/mitis.htm |website=Wild Singapore |access-date=3 September 2023}}</ref>

Flowers are purple and grow on hanging spikes.<ref name="WS"/> Its fruits turn dark purple or red when they are ripe, they are harmful to humans.<ref name="asdfkljasdfh8owe">Loureiro, João de. Flora Cochinchinensis 2: 569–570. 1790.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200027070  |title=Caryota mitis  |date=n.d. |website=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras |access-date=8 February 2014<!-- fr pg hstry -->}}</ref> The tree slowly deteriorates not long after it bears fruit.<ref name="WS"/>

==Uses==
Cultivated mainly as an ornament plant in [[Cambodia]], where it is named ''tunsaé töch'', traditional healers burn the heaps of felted hairs from the leaves' axils to treat ill limbs of patients.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dy Phon |first1=Pauline |title=Plants Utilised In Cambodia/Plants utilisees au Cambodge |date=2000 |publisher=Imprimerie Olympic |location=Phnom Penh |page=136|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=InD2RAAACAAJ|author1-link=Pauline Dy Phon }}</ref>

Its trunk [[pith]] can be extracted to make a kind of flour that has similar properties like [[sago]].<ref name="WS"/>

==Toxicity==
The fruit of ''C. mitis'' is saturated with [[raphides]], sharp, needle-shaped crystals of [[calcium oxalate]]. The raphides are strong irritants that cause damage and later itching upon contact with skin, and if ingested, the mouth. This is a result of the physical structure of the raphides, and not any chemical reaction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Snyder |first1=D S|last2=Hatfield |first2=G M |last3=Lampe |first3=K F |title=Examination of the itch response from the raphides of the fishtail palm Caryota mitis |journal=Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology |date=April 1979 |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=287–292 |doi=10.1016/0041-008x(79)90035-8|pmid=473178|bibcode=1979ToxAP..48..287S |hdl=2027.42/23600 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
